Well, there's where a particularly noteworthy fact comes in that few talk about: It doesn't have to be all or nothing.

Personally I fully understand the rationale behind copyright, and realize that it has been successful at what it is intended for. In fact, in some ways I might be for stronger copyright laws. However, those are contingent on some very important things, including:

  • A short copyright term - 5-10 years, maximum, and then it goes into the public domain
  • No further erosion of fair use, period
  • Sane penalties - you do not owe a record company hundreds of thousands of dollars for a few downloads that come off your computer, 1 download does not equal 1 lost sale, and you shouldn't go to jail for copyright infringement longer than rapists and murderers if you go into actual criminal infringement
  • No messing with computers to force copy protection or prevent modification
  • No bullshit licenses that erode property rights, e.g. you can't sell a car because the software was "only licensed" to you
  • The creators actually get a good chunk of this money that we're forking over - as-is, copyright primarily benefits the corporations while a lot of the artists and authors get peanuts

Additionally, rationalization does not mean that what is rationalized is in the least bit untrue. At this point, however, piracy can be considered a form of civil disobedience against a blatantly unjust and dangerous system. There are limits to how much you can practically do, especially when the Copyright Office is classifying large-scale disagreement with proposals to strengthen the DMCA as a DDoS. Arguably it also keeps the subject in the public eye, which is rather critical when our rights are being decided in back rooms filled with politicians and corporate sponsors (see: TPP and the other various "trade agreements" that are being put together to systematically sell us out in many ways, copyright law being one of them).

However, if it does come down to an all or nothing option, I choose nothing. Because while nothing is bad, "all" is downright disastrous, up to and including compromising our very political system, which might well end up manifesting with companies using their intellectual property as a way to force us into a situation with mega-corps like some sci-fi dystopia. The groundwork is already being laid, for all intents and purposes. Furthermore, it is highly unlikely that the copyright industry will accept any sort of compromise other than "compromises" that ultimately are gradual continued encroachment and control.

So. I'd be quite willing to entertain thoughts of actual compromise and improvement of the situation for both sides. However, in the current climate, we are being given a set of very bad options, so I'm going to choose the one that gives the most liberty, and IMNSHO does more to promote freedom of expression, innovation, and many other things we all care about.
